narrativeProgression.description: Dr. Doria transitions to a new problem that puzzled physicists and introduces the "Photoelectric Effect".
Dr. Doria engages the viewer by asking about Albert Einstein's Nobel Prize.
The famous equation "E=mc²" is corrected, highlighting that Einstein is best known for the "Theory of Relativity".
The "Photoelectric effect" is stated again for emphasis, and a visual appears on screen.
Dr. Doria begins a simplified explanation of the "Photoelectric Effect".
Heinrich Hertz, the scientist who first observed the "Photoelectric Effect" is introduced with a photo.
A basic animated visual of the "Photoelectric Effect" is displayed on screen.
Dr. Doria describes an experiment to make electrons come off metal faster, and how scientists originally thought that increasing the amplitude (brightness) of the light wave would achieve this.
A purple "X" appears on screen, highlighting that the scientist's original prediction is wrong.
Dr. Doria describes an experiment where scientists change the frequency (color) of light waves and predict it will have no effect on the photoelectric effect.
A purple "X" appears on screen, highlighting that the scientist's prediction is wrong again.
The unexpected results of the two experiments are summarized in text on the screen.
A video of waves crashing on the beach is used to illustrate the analogy of light waves being similar to water waves.
Dr. Doria explains how Albert Einstein's explanation of the Photoelectric Effect led to a Nobel Prize.
The animation of the light wave is replaced by an animation of green dots (photons) and the word "photons" appears below.
Dr. Doria explains how Einstein explained the color of light.
A purple arrow labeled "energy" points across the screen.
The animation with the light bulb, wavy line, platform, and three green spheres is shown again to further explain how higher energy light (blue light) knocks off more electrons.
The animation shows how red photons do not have enough energy to knock the electrons off the metal.
The equation "E=hv-Φ" appears.
The photo of Einstein with the Nobel Prize is shown.
Dr. Doria explains that the "Photoelectric Effect" is important in solar energy.
Dr. Doria explains that the "Photoelectric Effect" is used in night vision goggles.
Dr. Doria states that Einstein's theory that light can act as a particle called a photon is a "big step" in the creation of Quantum Mechanics.
Dr. Doria explains that Isaac Newton had a similar idea about light acting like particles hundreds of years before Einstein.
Dr. Doria poses the question of whether light is a particle or a wave.
The screen fades to black.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Hi, and welcome to my series of videos for physical chemistry 2.
In this course, we're looking at a completely new topic, quantum mechanics, the study of
the energy and motion of particles like electrons, and how they interact with each other and
with light.
The ideas we'll explore are the basis for our whole understanding of chemistry and how
atoms and molecules interact.
As we've discussed in class, prior to the theories of quantum mechanics, the motions
of particles like electrons and nuclei were thought to follow the laws of mechanics
described by Isaac Newton and Galileo, which we now call classical mechanics, to distinguish
it from quantum mechanics.
But as technology and our understanding of atomic and subatomic particles improved, physicists
began to realize that classical mechanics wasn't sufficient to explain their observations.
As we discussed in class, one of the phenomena that couldn't be explained by classical mechanics
was black body radiation.
Today, I want to tell you about another phenomena that puzzled physicists of the late 19th and
early 20th centuries, and how it moved us another step closer to the development of quantum
mechanics.
Today, I want to tell you a little about everybody's favorite scientist, Albert Einstein.
First two quick questions about him.
First question.
Did Albert Einstein ever receive a Nobel Prize?
If you said yes, you're absolutely right.
Einstein won the Nobel Prize for Physics in 1921.
So question number two, what theory did he propose that got him the Nobel Prize?
If you said the theory of relativity, believe it or not, you're actually wrong about that.
Nowadays, Einstein's most famous for the theory of relativity, but before he developed
that, he worked on some other tricky physics problems, including capillary action, and the
way particles move around in a fluid.
Another problem he worked on is called the photoelectric effect, and his theory of how
it works is actually what he won the Nobel Prize for.
Like a lot of good ideas, it's amazing how simple it is.
So what is the photoelectric effect?
Well back in 1887, Heinrich Hertz, the same guy whose name pops up in words like kilohertz
and megahertz when we talk about frequency, Heinrich Hertz noticed that if you shine ultraviolet
light on an electrode, it'll make electrical sparks more easily.
Basically, the light knocks off electrons from the metal in the electrode, and the electrons
cause the sparks that you see.
That doesn't sound too hard to understand, but if you actually start doing experiments,
you find out that the photoelectric effect doesn't behave the way you might expect it
would.
Now even back then, they knew that light was a wave, so they figured a light wave would
act something like a sound wave.
So for example, let's say you wanted the electrons to come off the metal moving faster.
In that case, you'd hit them with more energy.
Now if the wave was a sound wave, the way you'd make it have more energy is by increasing
the amplitude.
Basically, you'd make the sound louder.
So they thought that the same thing would happen if you increased the amplitude of a light
wave.
If you make a light wave's amplitude higher, you do that by making the light brighter.
But if you make the light brighter, that's not what happens.
If you make the light brighter, it doesn't change the speed of the electrons at all.
Instead, you just get more electrons coming off the metal.
Another odd thing happens if you change the frequency of the wave.
